_comment: Single source of truth for the South Tampa neighborhood catalog and detail pages. Personality copy is Kevin-supplied. `draft` fields are AI-written and marked unreviewed until Kevin confirms them through the weekly review form (see scripts/email_neighborhood_review.py and /neighborhood-review/). Run scripts/build_neighborhoods.py after any edit.

districts.name: Hyde Park & Northeast South Tampa
districts.blurb: The oldest, densest and most walkable corner of South Tampa. Brick streets, front porches, and the closest thing Tampa has to a genuine urban village.

districts.name: Palma Ceia & Central South Tampa
districts.blurb: The residential heart. Oak canopies, brick streets, A-rated schools and quiet prestige. This is what most people picture when they say South Tampa.

districts.name: Bayshore & Southeast South Tampa
districts.blurb: From the stately homes lining Bayshore Boulevard down through Ballast Point and the fast-changing Gandy corridor.

districts.name: Western & Waterfront South Tampa
districts.blurb: Big lots, mature landscaping and canal frontage. Where South Tampa gets quiet, private and boat-accessible.

districts.name: Port Tampa
districts.blurb: Old Florida, geographically and culturally its own thing. It started as a separate town and it still feels like one.

districts.name: South Tampa-Adjacent
districts.blurb: Frequently marketed as South Tampa, though locals will tell you these are northern-edge neighborhoods or separate areas entirely. Worth knowing before you tour.

historic-hyde-park.name: Historic Hyde Park
historic-hyde-park.personality: Classic, polished and walkable. Historic homes, shaded streets, front porches and a strong sense of old Tampa, with upscale shopping and dining nearby.

draft.take:
The brick streets are the first tell. Hyde Park was laid out before the car set the terms, so the blocks are short, the sidewalks are continuous, and the oak canopy meets overhead in a way newer parts of South Tampa cannot replicate. Front porches sit close to the street, alleys run behind many blocks, and the architecture reads as a record of the early twentieth century: bungalows, Colonial Revivals, Queen Annes and four squares standing next to one another rather than in matched rows.

The housing suits people who want to walk to dinner. Hyde Park Village anchors the retail and restaurant side, Bayshore Boulevard is the front yard for the southern edge, and Kate Jackson Park sits in the middle of the residential grid. Downtown and the Riverwalk are a short drive or a manageable bike ride, and MacDill commuters get a straight run down Bayshore or Dale Mabry. Much of this is a local historic district with design review, which is why the streetscape has stayed intact while other South Tampa blocks have turned over entirely.

The honest tradeoff is control. That same design review governs exterior changes, additions and demolition, so a renovation here is a longer conversation than it would be six blocks south. Lots are narrow, garages are detached or absent, and living in a walkable urban grid means car doors, event traffic and neighbors within earshot. Buyers who want a blank slate and a wide side yard are shopping in the wrong neighborhood.
draft.expect:
Flood exposure varies block to block, and that variation matters more here than the neighborhood average does. Most of South Tampa sits in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, and flood insurance is mandatory with a mortgage inside those zones; Tampa's CRS Class 5 rating earns a 25 percent NFIP premium discount for policies in flood zones, which softens the number without erasing it. Blocks closer to Bayshore and the water generally carry more exposure than interior streets, so an elevation certificate and a current flood determination should be pulled on any specific address rather than assumed from the surrounding area. The FEMA 50 percent rule is the other item to understand: in an A or V zone, repairs and improvements exceeding half the structure's value within a rolling twelve months trigger a requirement to bring the home up to current floodplain code, elevation included. On a 1920s house under historic design review, that intersection is where projects get complicated, and it is worth pricing before closing rather than after.

Lots are small by South Tampa standards and parking is largely on-street or in a rear alley space. Traffic pressure comes from the arterials, Kennedy, Platt, Howard and Armenia, and from Hyde Park Village on busy evenings. Gasparilla and other Bayshore events close streets and fill the neighborhood for the day. New construction is limited compared with the rest of South Tampa: the district accounts for very little of the roughly 231 permitted residential demolitions South Tampa averages each year, because historic designation restricts teardowns. What does change tends to be renovation, restoration and rear additions rather than replacement.
draft.investment:
Within ZIP 33606, which also covers Davis Islands, Harbour Island and SoHo, values sit toward the middle of the broader South Tampa range rather than at the top or bottom of it. What separates Hyde Park from most of the surrounding market is what buyers are actually paying for. Across much of South Tampa, an older low-lying home trades as land, with the structure treated as a cost to remove. Here the historic district makes demolition difficult, so the house itself carries real value, and a well-restored original with intact detail, a sound roof and updated systems commands attention that a deferred-maintenance house on the same street does not. Supply is fixed, which supports values over time but also means inventory is thin and good examples move quickly.

Due diligence should start with the property's status inside the district, whether it is treated as a contributing structure, and exactly what exterior work requires review. From there, pull the elevation certificate, the flood zone determination, current flood and wind premiums, and the permit history on any prior renovation. On houses of this age, the practical questions are plumbing, electrical, foundation, roof and window condition, plus whether the previous owner's improvements were permitted. Insurance is the line item that surprises people most, and it should be quoted for the specific address before the inspection period closes.
draft.best_for: Buyers who want a walkable historic street with real architecture and are willing to accept small lots, on-street parking and design review over the freedom to renovate or rebuild as they please.

hyde-park-village.name: Hyde Park Village
hyde-park-village.personality: Stylish, manicured and social. Boutique shopping, brunch, fitness studios, events and a luxury lifestyle atmosphere. It is technically a commercial district within Hyde Park rather than a separate residential neighborhood.

draft.take:
Walk two blocks in any direction from Snow Avenue and the pattern is clear: this is a shopping and dining district first, and a small, deliberately manicured one at that. Brick streets, low-rise storefronts, planted medians and a compact grid of boutiques, restaurants, fitness studios and a movie house give it the feel of an outdoor town center rather than a mall. Weekend mornings run on brunch and a market crowd, weekday evenings on patio tables and studio classes, and the calendar stays busy with programmed events.

It is worth being precise about what it is. Technically this is a commercial core inside the larger Hyde Park neighborhood, not a residential neighborhood of its own. Almost nobody buys a single-family house in the Village itself. What buyers are actually buying is proximity to it, meaning the bungalow and rowhouse blocks that surround it, the condo and townhome buildings at its edges, and the short walk to Bayshore Boulevard a few blocks south.

The tradeoff is straightforward. The closer a home sits to the Village, the more of the walkability it captures and the more of the activity it absorbs. Blocks immediately adjacent get valet traffic, event overflow, delivery trucks and people looking for a free parking space on a Saturday night. Two or three streets out, the oak canopy takes over and it gets quiet fast.
draft.expect:
Parking is the daily friction point. There is structured garage parking plus metered and residential street parking, and it tightens noticeably on weekend evenings and during events. Gasparilla and the Bayshore parade route effectively close the area to normal car movement for a day, which residents plan around rather than fight. Traffic funnels through a historic street grid that was never widened, so the brick blocks stay slow by design and cut-through driving is a recurring neighborhood complaint.

On the residential side, expect small lots, short setbacks, alleys behind many blocks and structures built long before modern floodplain code. Much of South Tampa sits in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, which makes flood insurance mandatory with a mortgage, and Tampa's CRS Class 5 rating earns a 25 percent NFIP premium discount inside those zones. Elevation varies block to block here, so the flood determination on a specific address matters more than any neighborhood-wide assumption. New construction is far more constrained than in the rest of South Tampa: the residential fabric around the Village falls largely within Hyde Park's locally designated historic district, where exterior changes and demolitions go through design review. South Tampa and Central Tampa together account for roughly 88 percent of the City's residential demolitions, at about 231 a year in South Tampa alone, but very little of that churn lands on these particular streets.
draft.investment:
Pricing in the 33606 ZIP sits in the middle of the overall South Tampa range, which understates what happens on the blocks closest to the Village. That ZIP also covers Davis Islands, Harbour Island, Hyde Park and SoHo, so the median blends very different products. Walkable historic Hyde Park inventory is limited by the historic district and by lot supply, and the well-restored examples tend to command a premium over comparable square footage further west where land is easier to replace.

The land-versus-house question plays out differently here than in most of South Tampa. Elsewhere, an older low-lying home often trades as a lot, in part because the FEMA 50 percent rule requires that a structure in an A or V zone be brought up to current floodplain code, including elevation, once repairs or improvements exceed half the structure's value on a rolling 12-month basis. In the historic district, tearing down and starting over is not a given, so the value of an existing structure and the cost of restoring it inside design review guidelines carry more weight. A buyer should pull the flood zone and elevation certificate for the specific address, confirm whether the property is contributing within the historic district, ask what has already been spent toward that 50 percent threshold, and check condo or townhome documents for insurance and reserve exposure.
draft.best_for: Buyers who want to live within walking distance of restaurants, shops and events and will accept parking pressure, event weekends and historic district review in exchange for the most walkable address in South Tampa.

soho.name: SoHo
soho.personality: Young, energetic and restaurant-driven. Popular with professionals who want nightlife and walkability, but not necessarily peace and quiet.

draft.take:
South Howard Avenue is the reason this pocket has a name of its own. The corridor runs thick with restaurants, bars and coffee counters, and the blocks feeding into it are narrow, gridded and shaded, with brick paving on many side streets and 1920s bungalows sitting close to the sidewalk behind low front porches. Bayshore Boulevard is a short walk south, Hyde Park Village a short walk east, and almost nothing here requires a car for the sake of dinner.

The housing stock reads as two overlapping layers. There are original frame and masonry bungalows, some restored to a high standard and some still waiting on it, and there is a steady layer of infill: skinny-lot single-family builds, townhome pairs and small attached projects squeezed onto platted lots that were never sized for three-car garages. The result suits professionals, couples and downsizers who value proximity over acreage, and it does not suit anyone who wants a yard with room to spare.

The honest tradeoff is noise. Living within walking distance of a restaurant and bar corridor means late traffic, valet activity, rideshare pickups and weekend volume, and it does not soften much on the blocks just off Howard. That energy is exactly what draws people here, and it is also the thing most likely to wear on a buyer who assumed the quiet would start one street back.
draft.expect:
Most of South Tampa sits in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, and flood insurance is mandatory with a mortgage inside those zones. Exposure varies block to block in this part of 33606, so an elevation certificate and a parcel-level zone check matter more than any neighborhood generalization. Tampa's CRS Class 5 rating earns a 25% NFIP premium discount inside flood zones, which helps, though insurance is still the line item that surprises people coming from outside Florida. The FEMA 50% rule also applies: in an A or V zone, repairs or improvements exceeding half the structure's value within a rolling 12 months trigger a requirement to bring the home up to current floodplain code, elevation included. That single rule shapes what is worth renovating on an older low-lying bungalow.

Lots are small and often narrow, with alleys behind some blocks and tight side setbacks throughout. Off-street parking is limited and street parking near the Howard corridor is contested, with residential permit restrictions in effect on some blocks, so confirming what a specific address actually has is worth doing before an offer. Howard and Armenia carry real traffic, and the one-way pairs running east and west through Hyde Park move faster than their width suggests. New construction is constant: South Tampa averages roughly 231 permitted residential demolitions a year and, with Central Tampa, accounts for about 88% of the City's residential demolitions, and infill here arrives one lot at a time rather than as subdivisions. Buyers should also verify whether a parcel falls inside a historic district boundary where exterior alterations are subject to review.
draft.investment:
Values in this ZIP sit in the middle of the South Tampa range, well above the lower-priced inland ZIPs and below the waterfront and island extremes, and the walkability premium is a real part of what buyers are paying for. Demand skews toward renters and owner-occupants who want the corridor at their doorstep, which supports both resale and lease interest, though the same nightlife adjacency narrows the buyer pool for anyone who needs quiet.

Whether a home trades on the house or on the land depends almost entirely on its condition and its flood zone. A well-restored or newly built elevated home trades on the house. An original bungalow low enough that the 50% rule constrains renovation tends to trade on the dirt, which is why so many of these lots turn over to builders. Due diligence worth doing before writing an offer: pull the flood zone and elevation certificate, confirm what is legally permitted on the lot given its size and any historic district overlay, verify off-street parking and permit-zone status, and get a current insurance quote rather than an assumption.
draft.best_for: Buyers who want to walk to dinner, live in an older gridded street pattern and accept weekend noise, tight lots and contested parking as the cost of being that close to the corridor.

hyde-park-spanishtown-creek.name: Hyde Park Spanishtown Creek
hyde-park-spanishtown-creek.personality: Historic, tucked away and slightly more eclectic than central Hyde Park. It feels like a hidden transition between downtown-oriented living and traditional residential streets.

draft.take:
The streets in this pocket run narrow and shaded, with brick underfoot in places, oaks meeting overhead, and front porches close enough to the sidewalk that neighbors actually talk from them. It reads as older and slightly looser than the showpiece blocks of central Hyde Park. Restored 1920s bungalows and Mediterranean Revival houses sit near small apartment buildings, converted duplexes, and the occasional modern infill, and the mix changes from one block to the next rather than settling into a single look.

Geographically it functions as a seam. Downtown, the University of Tampa, and the Kennedy corridor are close enough to reach on foot or by short drive, while a few turns in the other direction put you on residential streets that behave like traditional Hyde Park. Bayshore Boulevard, Hyde Park Village, and the SoHo restaurants are all within an easy walk or bike ride, which is the practical reason people accept the compromises that come with old housing stock.

The honest tradeoff is that the character is inseparable from the age. Small lots, tight setbacks, low finished-floor elevations, and creek-adjacent drainage come with the porches and the canopy. Buyers who want a large yard, a two-car garage, and a house built to current elevation standards will find those things easier to buy elsewhere in South Tampa.
draft.expect:
Like most of South Tampa, much of this area sits inside a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, and flood insurance is mandatory with a mortgage. Tampa's CRS Class 5 rating earns a 25 percent NFIP premium discount inside flood zones, which helps, but insurance is still the line item that surprises people, and older unelevated houses close to the tidal creek and the bay side carry more exposure than raised or newer construction a few blocks inland. Elevation certificates matter here, and they vary parcel to parcel. The FEMA 50 percent rule is the other thing to understand before planning a renovation: in an A or V zone, if improvements or repairs exceed half the structure's value within a rolling twelve months, the home has to be brought up to current floodplain code including elevation, which reshapes what a gut remodel actually costs.

Lots are small by South Tampa standards and many houses predate off-street parking, so street parking, alley access, and stacked driveways are normal. Streets are narrow, some are one-way, and traffic pressure comes from the surrounding arterials rather than from the residential blocks themselves. Event noise is real: Gasparilla and the Bayshore parade route, downtown events, and University of Tampa activity all register. South Tampa averages roughly 231 permitted residential demolitions a year and, with Central Tampa, accounts for about 88 percent of the City's residential demolitions, so infill and full renovations are a constant here. Portions of Hyde Park fall within designated historic districts where exterior work goes through review, and whether a specific parcel is covered should be confirmed before a buyer plans changes.
draft.investment:
Values sit in the middle of the 33606 range, a ZIP that also covers Hyde Park proper, Davis Islands, Harbour Island, and SoHo, so the ZIP-level number understates how wide the spread is within a few blocks. Restored and properly elevated historic homes trade well above the neighborhood's own middle, while older low-lying houses that cannot be renovated economically under the 50 percent rule often trade closer to what the land is worth. Walkability and proximity to downtown are the durable part of the value here; they are difficult to replicate anywhere else in South Tampa.

Due diligence should start with the flood zone, the elevation certificate, and the insurance quote in hand rather than estimated, followed by the permit history and any historic designation attached to the parcel. For anything bought as a renovation project, an early read on how the 50 percent rule applies to that specific structure is the difference between a cosmetic budget and an elevation budget.
draft.best_for: Buyers who want to walk to Hyde Park Village, Bayshore, and downtown from an older house with real character, and who will accept small lots, thin parking, and serious flood and renovation diligence to get it.

bayshore-gardens.name: Bayshore Gardens
bayshore-gardens.personality: Compact, central and convenient. A mixture of older homes, apartments, condominiums and townhomes close to Bayshore, Hyde Park and downtown.

draft.take:
The scale changes quickly here. One block holds small 1920s and mid-century houses with front porches and short driveways, the next holds a low-rise apartment building or a row of newer townhomes, and the blocks closest to Bayshore Boulevard pick up condominium buildings that look out over the water. That mix is unusual for South Tampa, where most pockets are uniformly single-family, and it is the main reason this corner reads as more urban than suburban.

What the location buys is time. Bayshore Boulevard and its balustrade sidewalk are a short walk or ride away, Hyde Park Village is close enough to reach on foot from parts of the neighborhood, downtown and the Riverwalk are a straight run up Bayshore, and MacDill commuters head the other direction on the same road or drop down Dale Mabry. Runners, cyclists and dog walkers use Bayshore constantly, and Gasparilla turns the waterfront edge into a staging ground for a weekend.

The tradeoff is consistency. Because the housing stock and ownership types vary lot by lot, the streetscape is not curated the way it is in Parkland Estates or Golfview, and rental density is higher. Buyers who want every neighbor's house to match theirs will find that frustrating; buyers who want a central address without the price of a large single-family lot will find it works in their favor.
draft.expect:
Like most of South Tampa, much of this area sits in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, and flood insurance is mandatory with a mortgage inside those zones. Tampa's CRS Class 5 rating earns a 25% NFIP premium discount for policies in flood zones, which helps, but insurance remains the line item that surprises people, particularly on older slab-on-grade houses near the Bayshore edge where surge exposure is highest. Exposure is not uniform: an upper-floor condominium and a 1940s cottage on a low block are two entirely different risk conversations, and the elevation certificate is what settles it.

Lots run small and shallow by South Tampa standards, so garages are rare, driveways are short, and street parking gets tight on blocks with apartments or duplexes. Traffic noise tracks how close a property sits to Bayshore, Howard or Bay to Bay, and the quieter interior streets are noticeably calmer than the arterial edges. New construction arrives one parcel at a time rather than in phases, usually as a tall single-family infill home or an attached townhome pair replacing something small. South Tampa and Central Tampa together account for roughly 88% of the City's residential demolitions, averaging about 231 permitted teardowns a year in South Tampa alone, and this neighborhood contributes its share.
draft.investment:
The ZIP sits at the top of the South Tampa range, but that figure is carried heavily by the larger-lot neighborhoods it also covers, including Palma Ceia, Golfview, Parkland Estates, Sunset Park and Virginia Park. In practice this pocket offers some of the lower entry points in that ZIP, because condominiums, townhomes and small older houses trade well below what a rebuilt single-family home on a full lot commands a few streets away. Proximity to Bayshore, Hyde Park and downtown is the durable part of the value here, and it is priced in.

On the single-family side, many older low-lying homes trade closer to land value than house value. The FEMA 50% rule is why: in an A or V zone, once repairs or improvements exceed half the structure's value within a rolling twelve months, the home has to be brought up to current floodplain code including elevation, which pushes buyers toward a rebuild rather than a renovation. A buyer should pull the flood zone and elevation certificate early, confirm what a full flood and wind quote actually costs before removing contingencies, and check setbacks and lot width against what can legally be built. On any older condominium building, the association's reserve study, milestone inspection status and master insurance policy deserve the same scrutiny as the unit itself.
draft.best_for: Buyers who want a central, walkable address near Bayshore and Hyde Park at a lower entry point than the surrounding single-family neighborhoods, and who accept a mixed streetscape, tight parking and real flood diligence as the price of that location.

dobyville-west-hyde-park.name: Dobyville / West Hyde Park
dobyville-west-hyde-park.personality: Historically significant, urban and rapidly changing. It has deeper cultural roots and more architectural variety than the polished sections of Hyde Park.

draft.take:
The street grid here is older and tighter than anything east of Howard, and it reads that way on foot: brick paving under the oaks, narrow lots, front porches close to the sidewalk, alleys behind. This is the historically Black side of Hyde Park, and the built record of that history is still visible in the small wood-frame cottages and shotgun-plan houses that sit next door to bungalows, brick four-squares, and new three-story townhomes. Architectural variety is the defining trait, not a single period look.

What the location buys is genuine walkability. Hyde Park Village, the Howard Avenue restaurant and bar strip, Kennedy Boulevard retail, the University of Tampa, and the Bayshore seawall are all reachable without a car, and downtown and Tampa General are a short drive or a bike ride. For MacDill commuters, the run down Bayshore or Dale Mabry is straightforward, though this is the northern end of South Tampa and the trip is longer than from Ballast Point or Bayshore Beautiful.

The honest tradeoff is that change is arriving fast and unevenly. A block can hold a restored century-old cottage, a vacant lot, and a just-completed townhome row at the same time. Buyers drawn to the neighborhood's texture should understand that the texture is actively being redrawn, and that the redrawing does not follow a predictable pattern from one street to the next.
draft.expect:
Lots are small by South Tampa standards, platted long before two-car garages, so parking is largely on-street or off an alley, and many older houses have no covered parking at all. Traffic is the price of being this close to everything: Howard and Armenia function as a one-way pair, Platt and Cleveland move east-west traffic through the area, Kennedy Boulevard carries volume at the north edge, and the Selmon Expressway is audible on the blocks nearest it. Portions of the area sit within historic district boundaries, so demolition, additions, and exterior changes may be subject to review, and that should be confirmed parcel by parcel rather than assumed.

On flood, most of South Tampa sits in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area and flood insurance is mandatory with a mortgage, but exposure here varies block by block and the elevation certificate on a specific address matters far more than a general impression of the neighborhood. Tampa's CRS Class 5 rating earns a 25 percent NFIP premium discount inside flood zones, which helps. For older low-slung houses in an A zone, the FEMA 50 percent rule is the constraint worth understanding early: once repairs or improvements exceed half the structure's value in a rolling 12-month period, the home must be brought up to current floodplain code, elevation included. That rule shapes what is realistic on a full renovation.
draft.investment:
Values sit in the middle of the South Tampa range rather than at the top, which is what makes the area interesting relative to the polished blocks of Hyde Park proper a few streets east. The premium here is on location and land, and a meaningful share of transactions are effectively land trades: South Tampa averages roughly 231 permitted residential demolitions a year and, with Central Tampa, accounts for about 88 percent of the City's residential demolitions, and this is one of the corners where that activity is most visible in new townhome and infill construction.

Because of that, two questions do most of the work. First, zoning and lot dimensions, since what can be built or added determines whether a buyer is paying for a house or for a development site. Second, historic designation status, which can limit demolition and exterior alteration on some parcels and not others within a short walk. Pulling the elevation certificate, the zoning designation, and any historic overlay on a specific address before writing an offer is the practical due diligence here.
draft.best_for: Buyers who want real walkability, brick streets, and architectural character close to downtown, and who accept small lots, street parking, traffic noise, and a neighborhood still visibly in the middle of redevelopment.

courier-city-oscawana.name: Courier City-Oscawana
courier-city-oscawana.personality: Dense, lively and urban. Apartments, townhomes, restaurants and older homes create a more active, less suburban version of South Tampa. Portions are included in District 4.

draft.take:
The grid here is tight and the blocks are short, which is the whole appeal. Streets run between Kennedy Boulevard and Swann, with the South Howard corridor cutting through the middle, so a walk out the front door can end at a restaurant patio, a coffee counter, or Hyde Park Village a few blocks east. Brick pavers survive on a number of streets, the oak canopy is mature, and Bayshore Boulevard is close enough to be a regular walking and running route rather than an occasional drive.

The housing stock is the most mixed in South Tampa. Original 1920s bungalows with deep front porches sit next to three-story townhome rows, small apartment buildings, and skinny new-build infill on split lots. That range means the neighborhood serves people at very different price points and life stages at the same time, and it reads as urban rather than suburban in a way almost nothing else south of Kennedy does.

The tradeoff is density itself. Buyers get walkability, a genuine street life, and a short trip to downtown and the Selmon, but they also get a neighbor's wall closer than they might expect, headlights in the bedroom window, and a bar crowd on Howard that does not go quiet early. Portions of the neighborhood fall inside District 4, and boundaries here should be confirmed address by address rather than assumed from the neighborhood name.
draft.expect:
Flood exposure varies more block to block here than in the waterfront pockets. Most of South Tampa sits in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, where flood insurance is mandatory with a mortgage, and Tampa's CRS Class 5 rating earns a 25% NFIP premium discount inside those zones. Some parcels in this part of the district sit on higher inland ground and carry a different designation, which changes the monthly number substantially, so the elevation certificate and flood determination deserve attention before the appraisal, not after. Insurance in general is the line item that surprises people moving in from outside Florida.

Lots are small and often narrow, a legacy of the original plats, and setbacks are minimal. Off-street parking is the practical constraint: some homes have a single pad or an alley space, some have nothing, and on-street parking near the Howard corridor competes with restaurant and bar traffic on weekend nights. Howard, Armenia, Platt and Kennedy all carry steady commuter volume, and Gasparilla weekend closes streets and fills every curb for blocks. New construction is constant. South Tampa averages roughly 231 permitted residential demolitions a year and, with Central Tampa, accounts for about 88% of the City's residential demolitions, and this neighborhood absorbs a visible share of that as older cottages come down for townhomes and taller single-family infill.
draft.investment:
Values sit in the middle of the South Tampa range, and the ZIP that covers this neighborhood also covers Hyde Park, Davis Islands, Harbour Island and SoHo, so ZIP-level figures blend very different products and should not be read as a comp. The more useful distinction is what a given sale is actually pricing. Renovated bungalows and newer townhomes trade on the structure. Small original cottages on walkable blocks frequently trade on the land, because the redevelopment math on a short walk to Howard and Hyde Park Village is straightforward for a builder.

The FEMA 50% rule is the specific thing to research on any older home in an A zone here: once repairs or improvements exceed 50% of the structure's value, with land excluded and costs accumulating over a rolling 12 months, the house must be brought up to current floodplain code including elevation. That single rule decides whether a cosmetic-looking project is a renovation or a teardown. Beyond that, buyers should look into zoning and permitted density on the parcel, whether the block is trending toward townhomes, HOA structure and reserves on attached product, and how the property's flood determination compares to the one next door.
draft.best_for: Buyers who want to walk to dinner, Hyde Park Village and Bayshore on a real urban grid, and will accept small lots, tight parking and audible nightlife as the price of that location.

davis-islands.name: Davis Islands
davis-islands.personality: Friendly, self-contained and waterfront-oriented. It has a small-town island personality, a neighborhood business district and a strong outdoor lifestyle despite being minutes from downtown.

draft.take:
Cross the bridge from Bayshore and the pace shifts. Davis Islands was dredged and platted in the 1920s as a self-contained resort development, and it still reads that way: a grid of short blocks, Mediterranean Revival stucco with barrel tile roofs, a real business district on East Davis Boulevard, and water at the end of most streets. Residents walk to dinner, to coffee, to the dog beach, to the tennis complex. Downtown is minutes away over the Davis Boulevard bridge, but the island does not feel like an extension of it.

The housing is a genuine mix. Original 1920s and 1930s Spanish-style homes and courtyard cottages sit near mid-century ranches, canal-front houses with private docks on the outer streets, and a growing number of tall elevated new builds replacing ground-level stock. It suits boaters, downtown and Tampa General commuters, and buyers who want walkability with a quieter, more residential feel than Hyde Park Village or SoHo. Marjorie Park Marina, the seaplane basin, the yacht club and Picnic Island-style shoreline access give the neighborhood an outdoor orientation that most inland South Tampa streets cannot match.

The honest tradeoff is access and exposure. There is essentially one way on and off the islands, so a stalled car or a shift change at Tampa General backs up the bridge approach. Being surrounded by water is the appeal and also the risk, and that shows up in insurance, in construction decisions, and in how a hurricane season is experienced here.
draft.expect:
Nearly all of the islands sit low and were built on fill, and like most of South Tampa the area falls within a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, which makes flood insurance mandatory with a mortgage. Tampa's CRS Class 5 rating earns a 25% NFIP discount inside flood zones, which helps, but insurance remains the line item that surprises people, particularly on older ground-level houses and on canal-front parcels where the zone designation can be more restrictive. The FEMA 50% rule matters here more than in most neighborhoods: once improvements or repairs exceed half the structure's value within a rolling 12 months, the home has to be brought up to current floodplain code, including elevation. That math is why so many original cottages come down instead of getting renovated in stages.

Lots are modest by South Tampa standards, with short setbacks, alleys behind some blocks, and driveways that hold fewer cars than a family typically owns. Street parking in the village fills up on weekend evenings. Expect small aircraft traffic from Peter O. Knight, seaplane activity in the basin, and medical helicopters serving Tampa General at the north end, all of which are normal background noise rather than occasional events. draft.investment:
Within ZIP 33606, which also covers Hyde Park, Harbour Island and SoHo, values sit around the middle of the broader South Tampa range, but the spread inside the islands themselves is wide. An interior block of original cottages and a canal-front street with deep water and a dock are different markets. Waterfront and dockable parcels price well above the neighborhood norm, and much of the older low-lying inventory trades closer to land value than to house value, because the practical path for a buyer is a full rebuild rather than a partial remodel.

Due diligence should start with the elevation certificate, the specific flood zone designation, and a current insurance quote rather than the seller's expiring policy. On waterfront, seawall condition, dock and lift permitting, and canal depth at low tide are worth verifying independently. Buyers planning to renovate should ask what permitted work has already been done and how it counts against the 50% threshold, and anyone planning a tall rebuild should confirm height and setback constraints given proximity to the airport and the neighborhood's historic-era platting. harbour-island.name: Harbour Island
harbour-island.personality: Polished, controlled and downtown-adjacent. More condominiums, townhomes and gated living than traditional neighborhood streets. Many people group it with South Tampa, although it feels more connected to downtown.

draft.take:
Almost nothing here predates the 1980s, and the island reads that way: curved private drives instead of a grid, guarded entries, mid-rise condominium buildings and townhome courts arranged around water frontage and a marina. There are no brick streets and no oak canopy on the island, which is the clearest way to understand how different it is from Hyde Park a mile west. The landscaping is palms, hedges and maintained common areas, and most of it is somebody's association responsibility rather than a homeowner's Saturday.

The orientation is downtown. A short walk over the Franklin Street bridge puts residents in Water Street, Sparkman Wharf, the Riverwalk and Amalie Arena, and the island has its own small grocery, athletic club and hotel, so daily life can be handled without a car. Bayshore Boulevard and the Kennedy corridor put MacDill within a straightforward commute, but the pull of the place is northward into the city core, not outward into the residential neighborhoods to the south.

The tradeoff is neighborhood texture. Buyers give up yards, front porches, garages that open onto a street and the loose sociability of a bungalow block, and they get security, water views, lock-and-leave maintenance and genuine walkability in return. Association fees are a permanent line item here, not an occasional one, and they carry the buildings, the grounds and the shared amenities.

Like most of South Tampa, the island sits in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, so flood insurance is mandatory with a mortgage, and Tampa's CRS Class 5 rating earns a 25 percent NFIP premium discount inside those zones. The exposure profile is different from an older low-lying street, though. Much of the island's residential product is newer, elevated, and built over podium or structured parking, which means ground-level garages, lobbies and storage are the vulnerable parts rather than living space. For attached homes, the master association policy and the reserve study matter as much as the individual unit policy, and the FEMA 50 percent rule that drives teardowns elsewhere in South Tampa rarely governs decisions here. The roughly 231 permitted residential demolitions South Tampa averages each year are happening on other streets.

Lots are small to nonexistent by South Tampa standards, and parking is assigned garage or deck space with limited guest capacity, so anyone hosting regularly should confirm what visitors are actually allowed to use. Traffic is the island's most quotable quirk: access is limited, and event nights at Amalie Arena, cruise days at the port and Gasparilla weekend all put pressure on the same few approaches. New construction is concentrated just off the island in the Water Street district, which brings amenities and crane activity in roughly equal measure.
draft.investment:
The 33602 ZIP that covers the island also takes in the downtown edge and North Hyde Park, so its median lands in the middle of the wide South Tampa range rather than at the top. That figure understates waterfront and view product on the island itself and overstates smaller interior units, which is a reminder that pricing here tracks building, floor, exposure and fee structure more than it tracks the ZIP. Homes trade on the residence, the view and the association, not on the dirt underneath, which is the reverse of how much of South Tampa's older housing stock is valued.

Due diligence is association due diligence. A buyer should read the reserve study, ask about recent and pending special assessments, confirm milestone inspection and structural reserve status for older mid-rise buildings, review the master flood and wind coverage, and understand rental restrictions if the unit is ever meant to generate income. Resale strength here has historically leaned on walkability to downtown and the water frontage, both of which are durable, but fee escalation and insurance costs are the variables worth modeling before committing.
draft.best_for: Buyers who want walkable, secured, low-maintenance living next to downtown and are willing to trade yards, brick streets and neighborhood texture for it, with association fees and event-night traffic as the standing cost.

palma-ceia.name: Palma Ceia
palma-ceia.personality: Quintessential South Tampa. Brick streets, mature oak trees, established homes and quiet prestige without feeling excessively flashy.

draft.take:
The streets do most of the talking here. Brick pavers, oak limbs meeting overhead, sidewalks that actually go somewhere, and a housing stock that reads as layers rather than one era: 1920s and 1930s bungalows and Mediterranean revivals, postwar ranches, and newer two-story custom builds on the same block. The Palma Ceia Golf and Country Club anchors the middle of it, Bay to Bay Boulevard carries the coffee shops and restaurants, and Bayshore Boulevard is close enough that walking or running it becomes routine rather than an outing. Hyde Park Village is a short ride east, and the MacDill commute is a straight shot down MacDill Avenue or Bayshore.

This is the part of South Tampa that suits buyers who want an established address without a gate or a high-rise. It works for families who want to stay put through school years, for buyers moving in from a condo or from out of state who want walkability, and for anyone who values a lot with mature trees over a new roof and a warranty. The prestige here is understated. Renovated bungalows sit next to houses that have not been touched since the 1960s, and nobody seems to mind.

The honest tradeoff is that the character comes with age. Older homes on small lots mean original plumbing and electrical, tight closets, single-car garages or none, and additions that were permitted decades ago under different rules. Buyers who want turnkey square footage generally end up either paying up for a recent build or planning a renovation from the start.

Tampa's CRS Class 5 rating earns a 25 percent NFIP premium discount inside flood zones, which helps, but insurance overall is the line item that surprises people relocating here. Parking is mostly driveway and street, and the narrower brick blocks fill up when a house is entertaining. Positioned at the top of the South Tampa range, this is one of the addresses that sets the ceiling rather than follows it. Demand is broad because the appeal is not tied to a single feature, and inventory of genuinely well-kept older homes on good streets stays thin. That combination keeps well-presented listings moving.

Much of what changes hands here trades on the land as much as the house. The FEMA 50 percent rule is the reason: in an A or V zone, once repairs or improvements exceed half the structure's value, with costs accumulating over a rolling 12 months and land excluded, the home has to be brought up to current floodplain code including elevation. That math pushes many older low-lying houses toward demolition rather than remodel, and buyers planning a substantial renovation should price that scenario before writing an offer. Worth investigating on any specific property: the flood zone and elevation certificate, permit history on prior additions, whether the street and its pavers are city maintained, protected trees on the lot, and what the setbacks and lot coverage rules would actually allow if the plan is to build.
draft.best_for: Buyers who want the classic brick-street, oak-canopy South Tampa address and are willing to pay top-of-market for it, and to take on an older home's condition and flood-zone homework in exchange.

palma-ceia-pines.name: Palma Ceia Pines
palma-ceia-pines.personality: Eclectic, connected and urban-residential. It mixes houses, apartments, businesses, schools and churches, creating a more varied atmosphere than traditional Palma Ceia.

A postwar ranch can sit across the street from a small apartment building, with a church lot on the corner and an office or storefront a block over where the grid meets the arterials. Nothing about it reads as curated, and that is the point: this is a working residential pocket of central South Tampa that absorbs its commercial edges rather than walling them off.

The result suits people who want a central address and a short commute more than they want architectural uniformity. MacDill commuters, Westshore and airport workers, and anyone who wants Hyde Park Village, Bayshore Boulevard and the Gandy crossing all within an easy drive tend to do the math and land here. Housing runs the full spread, from modest older single-family homes to renovated mid-century houses to newer infill builds on the same street, and rentals sit in the mix rather than off to one side.

The honest tradeoff is predictability. Streets closer to Bayshore hold a tighter oak canopy and a more consistent look; the variety here means a quiet interior block can be one turn from steady traffic, and the parcel next door may carry different zoning than the house being purchased. Anyone who needs every neighbor to match should look south and east and expect to pay for that consistency.

palma-ceia-west.name: Palma Ceia West

That range is what makes the area work for a wider set of budgets than the surrounding streets in this part of South Tampa.

Deciding which version of the neighborhood is being bought matters more than any other choice on the block.

interbay.name: Interbay

interbay-south-of-gandy.name: Interbay-South of Gandy
interbay-south-of-gandy.personality: Outdoorsy, convenient and increasingly residential. Access to Gadsden Park and the Greenway adds an active lifestyle component.

macdill-air-force-base-area.name: MacDill Air Force Base Area

Access is by gate and credential. What matters to a buyer is everything that grows up around it.

Businesses along the lower Dale Mabry and Interbay corridors are built for the schedule of people who report to a gate in the morning: barbers, gyms, quick lunch counters, auto shops, banks with military lending desks. Neighborhoods within a short drive of the gates, including Interbay, Port Tampa, Ballast Point and the Gandy corridor, carry a steady undercurrent of PCS turnover, mid-lease relocations and buyers using VA financing. The honest tradeoff is that the base gives the surrounding area its reliability and also its constraints. Proximity to a gate is a durable amenity that does not depend on a market cycle. Whether a given property trades on the house or the land depends almost entirely on elevation and age. That math is what pushes many of these houses toward replacement rather than renovation. Due diligence should include the flood zone determination and elevation certificate, a current insurance quote rather than an estimate, the AICUZ noise and accident-potential mapping, and confirmation of which gate an address actually routes to during peak hours.
draft.best_for: Buyers who want proximity to the gate, a practical street feel and a dependable rental profile should focus on the neighborhoods ringing the base rather than expecting to live on it, and should treat aircraft noise, gate-hour traffic and flood insurance as the standing cost of that convenience.
